title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median home value across counties in Illinois state, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                       myvarE myvarM  popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                       <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 17001 Adams County, Illinois     155900   4554 65166    NA
2 17003 Alexander County, Illinois  58700  10578  5042    NA
3 17005 Bond County, Illinois      133100  13683 16627    NA
4 17007 Boone County, Illinois     198600   8350 53316    NA
5 17009 Brown County, Illinois     142200  19435  6320    NA
6 17011 Bureau County, Illinois    121900   3733 33027    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         49        240766.
2 Low confidence           2          4332.
3 Moderate                51         17381.


Average population in high confidence counties is the largest (240,766 people) compared to the other groups. On the other hand, the low confidence counties have the smallest average population with 4,332 people. Small counties tend to have low confidence reliability, while large counties tend to have high confidence reliability

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Census data is commonly used by policymakers as a source to develop programs. However, not all policies are perfectly suited to every area. There are many reasons for this. From an analytical perspective, understanding data sources reliability is important for identifying the limitations of an analysis and knowing how to address them, so we could get a better understanding of places to make a better decision. The ACS uses sampling methods to get estimation number. Therefore, it has a margin of error (MOE), which represents the range of uncertainty of an estimate.
Looking at median home value data from the ACS 5-year estimates for Illinois, the MOE percentage varies from 0.6% to 34.1%. With the largest MOE percentage (34.1%), Hardin County is the area about which we have the least certainty. There is a pattern in which low confidence reliability counties has the least average population, when high confidence reliability counties has the highest. Because the ACS uses sampling methods, smaller places yield smaller samples, which tend to result in lower reliability.
Understanding data reliability is important. If not, we may treat data from all counties as equally certain and apply policies without considering that data from smaller counties may be less representative of actual conditions. In this case, relying solely on median home value data in Illinois without considering its reliability could lead to housing assistance program application that are not well suited to Hardin County or other lower confidence counties, and smaller communities may continue to be disadvantaged.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Lubrano, Alfred’s article compares the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates and claims that several neighbourhoods experienced a noticeable increase in poverty rate. To verify the claim, I use the same ACS data and time period at the census tract level, as a proxy for the neighbourhood (since neighbourhood is not a formal census geography), so my numbers will not match its figures. The poverty rate is the number of people below the poverty level divided by the total population; therefore, I pull table B07012_002, which represents the population below 100 percent of the poverty level, and B07012_001, which represents the total population.
Because the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 time periods do not overlap, the two estimates come from independent samples, so the standard error of the difference is the square root of the sum of the squared standard errors. If the periods did overlap, some of the data in the second period would be redundant with the first, which would not completely capture the change over time.

Part 2 — Test
Rates, MOEs, and reliability
I calculate data reliability using the Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable. As a result, in the 2013–2017 data there are 8 reliable, 335 somewhat reliable, and 21 unreliable census tracts. There are 8 census tracts that present as NA; those census tracts have no population because they are airports, stadiums, or industrial areas. Part 3 — Adjudicate
The general idea that some places in Philadelphia are experiencing an increase in poverty while others are decreasing is supported by the data. Of the 63 statistically significant change tracts, meaning tracts that show a change big enough and clear enough to trust and not just something that could be random noise in the survey, 36 tracts show an increase and 27 show a decrease in poverty rate.
The map showing more areas in Philadelphia with increasing poverty rates could not supported by the data without telling about its reliability. There are only 63 statistically significant change tracts and 313 tracts show no change we can be sure is real rather than just noise, which risks leading readers to think more parts of Philadelphia are getting poorer than they actually are. This could affect decisions about where to live or invest because people might avoid or worry about neighborhoods that are actually stable, just because the article made it sound like poverty was spreading everywhere.
The neighborhood claims cannot be determined, because the article never explains which Census tracts were combined together to create the neighborhood boundaries.

Comparing Census data from 2006–2010 to 2013–2017, poverty went up in some parts of Philadelphia and down in others. Out of 376 census tracts examined, just 63 had a shift large enough, in which 36 areas got poorer, while 27 decrease in poverty rate. The other 313 tracts showed no change significant enough to say anything really changed, because it could just be noise in how the data was collected. It’s also worth noting that 8 tracts across the city have essentially no residential population which are places like airports and industrial land. However, beyond paying attention to the 36 tracts with significantly increased poverty rates, interventions should follow further investigation, taking data reliability into account across the wider set of tracts as well.

text:
Lubrano, Alfred’s article compares the 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 ACS 5-year estimates and claims that several neighbourhoods experienced a noticeable increase in poverty rate. To verify the claim, I use the same ACS data and time period at the census tract level, as a proxy for the neighbourhood (since neighbourhood is not a formal census geography), so my numbers will not match its figures. The poverty rate is the number of people below the poverty level divided by the total population; therefore, I pull table B07012_002, which represents the population below 100 percent of the poverty level, and B07012_001, which represents the total population.
Because the 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 time periods do not overlap, the two estimates come from independent samples, so the standard error of the difference is the square root of the sum of the squared standard errors. If the periods did overlap, some of the data in the second period would be redundant with the first, which would not completely capture the change over time.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate
The general idea that some places in Philadelphia are experiencing an increase in poverty while others are decreasing is supported by the data. Of the 63 statistically significant change tracts, meaning tracts that show a change big enough and clear enough to trust and not just something that could be random noise in the survey, 36 tracts show an increase and 27 show a decrease in poverty rate.
The map showing more areas in Philadelphia with increasing poverty rates could not supported by the data without telling about its reliability. There are only 63 statistically significant change tracts and 313 tracts show no change we can be sure is real rather than just noise, which risks leading readers to think more parts of Philadelphia are getting poorer than they actually are. This could affect decisions about where to live or invest because people might avoid or worry about neighborhoods that are actually stable, just because the article made it sound like poverty was spreading everywhere.
The neighborhood claims cannot be determined, because the article never explains which Census tracts were combined together to create the neighborhood boundaries.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
Comparing Census data from 2006–2010 to 2013–2017, poverty went up in some parts of Philadelphia and down in others. Out of all census tracts examined, just 63 had a shift large enough, in which 36 areas got poorer, while 27 decrease in poverty rate. The other 313 tracts showed no change significant enough to say anything really changed, because it could just be noise in how the data was collected. It’s also worth noting that in 2013-2017 data, 8 tracts across the city have essentially no residential population which are places like airports and industrial land. However, beyond paying attention to the 36 tracts with significantly increased poverty rates, interventions should follow further investigation, taking data reliability into account across the wider set of tracts as well.

text:
Part 7: Reflection
The feature that helped the most is the distance rings (core, inner, outer). They lowering the CV RMSE from 11.35 for the baseline to 10.86. Poverty is highest in the inner ring and lower in the core and outer areas, and rings capture better than the original variable distance to city hall. The feature that disappointed me most was theft density. Taking its log left the error at 11.35, the same as the baseline. Theft is high in Center City might be because of shoppers and tourists, not because residents are poor. The final model, which added thefts and bus stops, reached 10.87, so it is no better than the rings alone.
The coefficient for median age in the final model is -0.320. The β̂ reading is that, holding the other variables constant, each extra year of median age is associated with a 0.32 percentage point lower poverty rate. The ŷ reading is that if two similar tracts differ by 10 years in median age, the model predicts the older tract to have a poverty rate about 3.2 points lower.
The final residual map still shows red clusters in north and west Philadelphia, almost the same as the baseline. Next, I would measure housing, such as renter share, vacant buildings, and subsidized housing. Renter share is available in the ACS, and vacancy and property data are available from OpenDataPhilly.
The last plot shows that a reliable ACS number does not always mean a small miss. Some tracts with a low CV still have misses of 20 points or more, that means the model might missing something important about those areas, like housing or jobs, and it is not just a survey mistake. Tracts with a very high CV also have bigger misses, so some of that error may come from an uncertain ACS number.

Part 6: Fit vs. prediction






WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(5080)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[-train_idx, ] #the one that not in train

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

6B: 10-fold cross-validation
caret wants a plain data frame, so drop the geometry first. (The geometry isn’t a predictor, and train() will choke on it.)

               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m2 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 8: The Challenge
Your team’s job: build the best model for predicting tract median rent, then use it to answer the agency’s question.

Rules

The grade is 10-fold CV RMSE. Use model_df (or tracts) and run set.seed(5080) directly before train(), exactly as in Part 6B, so every team is tested on the same folds.
Don’t drop rows. If you add a variable with missing values, you change the folds and the comparison stops being fair. Fill the gaps or choose a different variable.
You may add any ACS variables (use load_variables(2023, "acs5") to browse) and any spatial feature you can build with Week 4 tools: distances, buffers, counts.
You may not use anything built from rent itself. That rules out med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden (B25071), and the rent distribution tables (B25063). Ask yourself: would the agency have this variable for a tract whose rent it’s trying to predict? If not, using it is cheating the test. That’s called leakage.



Deliver

Your CV RMSE, in dollars, written as a sentence.
One feature you added, and why. What did you think it would capture that the census variables miss? Did it help?
One coefficient, read twice. Pick a variable in your final model and give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
The agency’s list. Using your final model fit to all tracts, find the five tracts with the largest positive residuals (rent well above expectation). For each, report the residual and the rent CV. Which of the five would you tell the agency to trust, and which might be fog?
Your residual map. Did your added features make the clusters from Part 7B shrink?
